stage_description: The senior stage generally begins around fifteen years of age, though many horses stay active and useful well into their twenties with good care. Aging brings gradual changes: loss of muscle and topline, a rougher or greying coat, stiffer joints, failing teeth, and a weaker immune system. Older horses are prone to PPID (equine Cushing's disease) and to gaining or losing weight, so the aim of care is early detection and keeping the horse comfortable.
nutrition: Forage stays the foundation, but aging teeth may struggle with long-stem hay; softer forage, chopped hay, soaked hay pellets, or a complete senior feed can help hold weight. Always provide fresh water — important for reducing colic risk — and free-choice salt. Feeds designed for seniors are easier to chew and digest; adjust the ration with your veterinarian to hold a healthy body condition.
activity: Keep senior horses moving with daily turnout and light, regular exercise suited to their soundness, since gentle movement eases stiff joints and maintains muscle. Provide shelter from cold, wind, and heat, because older horses regulate temperature less well, and let a stiff or arthritic horse warm up slowly before any work.
veterinary_check_frequency: Senior horses benefit from a wellness examination at least twice a year, as problems develop faster with age; these visits may include bloodwork to screen for PPID and other conditions, along with core vaccinations and deworming. Keep farrier visits every six to eight weeks and schedule dental exams at least yearly, or more often if the teeth are failing.
dental_care: Dental care is critical in old age: teeth wear down, loosen, or fall out, making chewing difficult and raising the risk of choke and colic. A veterinary dental exam at least once a year — sometimes more — allows careful floating (rasping) and lets the vet shift the diet to soft or complete feeds when a horse can no longer chew hay well.
warning_signs: Call a veterinarian for weight loss despite good feeding, a long or curly coat that fails to shed together with excessive drinking and urination (possible PPID), quidding or difficulty chewing, chronic lameness, or laminitis-like foot soreness. Colic signs — pawing, rolling, not eating, or looking at the flank — are always an emergency.
source_name: AAEP Senior Horse Care & PetMD (Kaela Schraer DVM)
